meta.referenceSelection: Per topic: top 14 matched citation counts, 10 newest precisely dated matched works, plus editorial readings; deduplicated.

routes.intro: How can an agent pursue the intended goal when rewards, instructions and feedback only describe it imperfectly? This topic follows the gap between measured success and desired behavior, including reward hacking, unintended side effects and goals that fail to generalize.
routes.boundary: Alignment concerns what the agent optimizes. Permissions limit what it can do; monitoring checks what it actually does. These can support alignment without establishing it.
questions: Can a coding agent improve test scores while violating the user’s actual requirements?
Does safe behavior survive changes in tasks, tools and feedback?

readings.why: Organizes accident risks around objectives, supervision and learning; a useful conceptual starting point.
readings.title: Concrete Problems in AI Safety

readings.why: Separates the observed reward from a hidden performance function, making specification failures measurable.
readings.title: AI Safety Gridworlds

routes.angle: Does optimizing the measured goal still serve the user?

routes.intro: Safe RL learns a useful policy while respecting safety constraints during training and execution. The central design choice is what must be bounded: expected cumulative cost, the probability of failure, or every individual action.
routes.boundary: A bound on expected cost is different from a guarantee that no unsafe action occurs. Check the environment model, constraint definition and assumptions before comparing methods.
questions: Can a policy remain safe when dynamics or constraints change?
How much reward and exploration efficiency are lost for each safety requirement?

readings.why: Introduces constrained policy search with near-constraint satisfaction per iteration under its assumptions.
readings.title: Constrained Policy Optimization

readings.why: Uses a synthesized shield to restrict or correct actions against a temporal-logic specification.
readings.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning via Shielding

routes.angle: Learn a policy while respecting explicit safety constraints.

routes.intro: This topic asks how a deployment can remain safe when an agent may strategically hide undesirable behavior or subvert its checks. It studies both evidence of deceptive behavior and protocols that limit harm from an untrusted model.
routes.boundary: A constructed deceptive model demonstrates a failure mode; it does not establish how often naturally trained systems deceive. Control protocols should be tested against adaptive attempts to defeat them.
questions: Can the actor and its monitor share the same blind spots?
Which auditing and editing protocols remain useful when the actor knows the defense?

readings.why: Turns intentional subversion into a protocol evaluation problem with trusted and untrusted models.
readings.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

readings.why: Constructs persistent backdoors and tests whether safety training removes them.
readings.title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training

routes.angle: Study what happens when the agent itself is untrusted.

routes.intro: Agents delegate effort but can also displace human choice. Research here asks when to request approval, how to preserve interruption and correction, and how a person can meaningfully control a long-running task.
routes.boundary: An approval button does not establish meaningful control. The human needs enough information, time and an effective way to change the outcome.
questions: Which irreversible actions require informed approval before execution?
Does an agent preserve the user’s ability to interrupt, revise and revoke delegation?

readings.why: Models incentives to preserve or disable a human off-switch and the role of uncertainty about objectives.
readings.title: The Off-Switch Game

readings.why: Shows how limited trusted human effort can be allocated within a control protocol.
readings.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

routes.angle: Decide when and how a person should stay in control.

routes.intro: Oversight evaluates and redirects an agent when a human cannot inspect every step. Assurance organizes evidence for a safety claim. Together they ask who checks the agent, what that checker can observe, and why the resulting evidence should be trusted.
routes.boundary: A strong judge on ordinary tasks may still miss the actor’s failures. Measure correlated errors, audit budgets and performance against deliberate evasion.
questions: What complementary information lets a weaker monitor catch a stronger agent?
Can assurance evidence remain valid after the model or toolchain changes?

readings.why: Proposes debate as a way to help a limited judge assess more complex claims.
readings.title: AI safety via debate

readings.why: Evaluates oversight inside an adversarial deployment protocol rather than only as isolated classification.
readings.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

readings.why: Study an implemented guard-agent approach before deciding what information your supervisor must observe.
readings.title: GuardAgent: Safeguard LLM Agents via Knowledge-Enabled Reasoning

routes.angle: Make limited supervision useful against stronger agents.

routes.intro: Runtime monitoring observes an agent’s trajectory and intervenes before or after risky steps. Monitors may inspect inputs, tool calls, generated code or state changes; the useful unit of analysis is the action sequence and its consequences.
routes.boundary: A detector’s accuracy alone does not describe a deployed monitor. Timing, false alarms, evasion, latency and what happens after an alert all matter.
questions: Can monitoring catch a harmful trajectory before an irreversible action?
How should monitoring trade off false alarms, latency and missed failures?

readings.why: Provides a clear intervention model: inspect proposed actions and enforce a stated safety specification.
readings.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning via Shielding

readings.why: Combines input detection, alignment checks and code analysis in an agent guardrail framework.
readings.title: LlamaFirewall: An open source guardrail system for building secure AI agents

readings.why: AgentSpec uses explicit triggers, predicates and enforcement rules for runtime constraints; compare this design with a learned monitor.
readings.title: AgentSpec: Customizable Runtime Enforcement for Safe and Reliable LLM Agents

readings.why: A guard agent checks user-defined requirements with knowledge-enabled reasoning, offering a concrete separate-monitor design.
readings.title: GuardAgent: Safeguard LLM Agents via Knowledge-Enabled Reasoning

routes.angle: Detect unsafe behavior and intervene during execution.

routes.intro: Formal approaches express a safety property precisely and prove or check it under explicit assumptions. The challenge is connecting the mathematical model to an agent’s changing tools, observations and environment.
routes.boundary: Verified code or a checked rule does not automatically verify the full agent. State which components, transitions and environmental assumptions the guarantee covers.
questions: Can natural-language policies be translated into correct executable constraints?
What happens when the real environment violates the proof assumptions?

readings.why: Connects temporal-logic safety specifications with an executable action shield.
readings.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning via Shielding

readings.why: Explores policy reasoning and verification tools for agent trajectories; inspect the scope of each checked claim.
readings.title: ShieldAgent: Shielding Agents via Verifiable Safety Policy Reasoning

routes.angle: Express the assumptions under which a guarantee holds.

routes.intro: Prompt injection occurs when content that an agent should treat as data influences its instructions or actions. Indirect injection places that content in a webpage, document or tool result the agent encounters while carrying out a legitimate task.
routes.boundary: Distinguish the attacker’s control over external content from the user’s legitimate authority. A successful defense must preserve useful task completion while preventing the attacker’s objective.
questions: Can instruction provenance survive retrieval, summaries, memory and delegated tools?
Do defenses hold under adaptive attacks at the same task utility?

readings.why: An early systematic study of indirect injection through retrieved content and connected applications.
readings.title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection

readings.why: Makes agent utility and adversarial robustness measurable in an extensible tool environment.
readings.title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents

readings.why: CaMeL separates trusted control flow from untrusted data and enforces capabilities around tool calls; its evaluation includes AgentDojo.
readings.title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design

routes.angle: Keep external content from becoming an instruction.

routes.intro: Jailbreak research examines attempts to make a model or agent comply with requests that its safety policy should reject. For tool-using agents, the outcome can include a completed sequence of harmful actions rather than only a harmful answer.
routes.boundary: Prompt injection concerns a trust boundary in external content; a jailbreak concerns bypassing behavioral restrictions. They can overlap, but require different attacker models and success criteria.
questions: Does a jailbreak preserve the capabilities needed to finish a harmful multi-step task?
How do refusal behavior and actual tool actions diverge?

readings.why: Establishes an influential automated adversarial-suffix approach; useful background for later agent attacks.
readings.title: Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models

readings.why: Measures malicious multi-step agent tasks together with retained capability after jailbreaking.
readings.title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents

routes.angle: Test the boundary between a request and a disallowed action.

routes.intro: Agents can access private context, retrieve documents and transmit information through tools. This topic studies which data may be used or disclosed, to whom, and under what purpose and consent constraints.
routes.boundary: Training-data extraction, context leakage and unauthorized tool-based exfiltration have different entry points. Identify the sensitive asset and the path that moves it before selecting a defense.
questions: Can an agent enforce purpose limits across multiple tools and recipients?
How can leakage be measured without exposing real private data?

readings.why: Demonstrates extraction of memorized training examples; background for understanding one source of leakage.
readings.title: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models

readings.why: Includes private-data exfiltration through tool-integrated agents under indirect injection.
readings.title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents

routes.angle: Trace where private information can leave an agent workflow.

routes.intro: Retrieval and persistent memory give an agent useful context, but can also carry poisoned instructions or false beliefs across tasks. Research follows how content is admitted, retrieved, trusted, updated and forgotten.
routes.boundary: A poisoned document, a corrupted memory and a misleading summary have different persistence and control assumptions. Evaluate effects over later tasks, not only the initial encounter.
questions: Can a single interaction contaminate later decisions after the source disappears?
What evidence is needed to admit, revise or delete a memory?

readings.why: Studies targeted poisoning of an agent’s memory or knowledge base and its retrieval conditions.
readings.title: AgentPoison: Red-teaming LLM Agents via Poisoning Memory or Knowledge Bases

readings.why: Explains why retrieved text can cross the boundary between data and instructions.
readings.title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection

readings.why: MemoryGraft studies poisoned experience retrieval and reports persistent effects across sessions, extending the reading route beyond knowledge-base poisoning.
readings.title: MemoryGraft: Persistent Compromise of LLM Agents via Poisoned Experience Retrieval

routes.angle: Understand attacks that persist through retrieved memories.

routes.intro: An agent depends on models, packages, tool servers, skills and their descriptions. Supply-chain research examines how a compromised dependency or an untrusted update can gain influence over the agent and its environment.
routes.boundary: A protocol implementation is only one part of the chain. Track provenance, versions, trust in providers and changes to permissions; one vulnerable example does not establish the prevalence of a vulnerability.
questions: Can tool descriptions or updates silently change the effective trust boundary?
How can agents verify the origin and intended permissions of third-party skills?

readings.why: An early audit of security issues in connected MCP workflows, useful for defining trust boundaries.
readings.title: MCP Safety Audit: LLMs with the Model Context Protocol Allow Major Security Exploits

readings.why: Offers privilege-control mechanisms relevant to limiting the impact of untrusted tools.
readings.title: Progent: Securing AI Agents with Privilege Control

routes.angle: Follow trust across tools, dependencies and extensions.

routes.intro: Tool safety asks whether an agent’s concrete actions are valid, authorized and safe in context. The research unit includes arguments, execution state, external side effects and recovery after a partially completed action.
routes.boundary: Correct text is insufficient if execution changes the wrong resource. Separate proposed actions, executed actions and observed outcomes, especially for irreversible operations.
questions: How can a system validate risky actions before they affect the real environment?
Can agents recover safely from timeouts, retries and partial completion?

readings.why: Uses an emulated tool sandbox to study difficult-to-stage agent failures and their evaluation.
readings.title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox

readings.why: Organizes diverse interactive environments and failure modes for agent safety evaluation.
readings.title: Agent-SafetyBench: Evaluating the Safety of LLM Agents

readings.why: AgentSpec makes execution constraints explicit; inspect its code-agent setting separately from embodied and driving experiments.
readings.title: AgentSpec: Customizable Runtime Enforcement for Safe and Reliable LLM Agents

routes.angle: Make risky actions observable, bounded and recoverable.

routes.intro: This topic asks who an agent is acting for and which operations it may perform. It covers delegated authority, least privilege, access policies and how authorization changes as a task proceeds.
routes.boundary: Authentication identifies a principal; authorization constrains an action. A valid login does not imply permission to use every tool or disclose every accessible item.
questions: Can permissions be bound to a task, recipient and duration?
Does delegation between agents amplify authority beyond the original user’s intent?

readings.why: Makes tool-use privileges explicit and enforces them around an agent’s execution.
readings.title: Progent: Securing AI Agents with Privilege Control

readings.why: Translates guard requests into executable checks, including access-control scenarios.
readings.title: GuardAgent: Safeguard LLM Agents by a Guard Agent via Knowledge-Enabled Reasoning

readings.why: CaMeL connects data-flow restrictions with tool capabilities, a useful comparison for privilege-control approaches.
readings.title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design

routes.angle: Limit what an agent is allowed to do, even if it is misled.

routes.intro: Embodied agents act through robots or other physical systems, where mistakes can cause collision, injury or damage. Safe learning, perception uncertainty and physical constraints must work together across the control loop.
routes.boundary: A safe plan in a language model does not guarantee safe motion. Distinguish high-level intent, low-level control, sensing assumptions and the simulator-to-reality gap.
questions: Can perception uncertainty be carried into action constraints?
How are safe stops and fallback controllers verified in changing environments?

readings.why: Connects policy optimization to explicit safety constraints, illustrated with simulated robot locomotion.
readings.title: Constrained Policy Optimization

readings.why: Shows how action-level enforcement can complement a learned controller under stated assumptions.
readings.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning via Shielding

routes.angle: Connect learned decisions to physical-world safety.

routes.intro: Safety can fail through interactions even when individual agents appear competent. This topic studies miscoordination, conflict, collusion, communication attacks and how failures propagate through a network of agents.
routes.boundary: More agents do not automatically provide independent checks. Shared models, information and incentives can create correlated errors or coordinated undesirable behavior.
questions: When does communication improve reliability, and when does it spread a failure?
How can evaluations detect collusion or hidden conflicts of interest?

readings.why: An influential interaction-based oversight proposal; study the judge and incentive assumptions.
readings.title: AI safety via debate

readings.why: Organizes multi-agent risks into miscoordination, conflict and collusion with shared risk factors.
readings.title: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI

routes.angle: Examine risks introduced by agents interacting with agents.

routes.intro: Safety evaluation turns a claim into testable tasks, threat models and outcome measures. A useful evaluation distinguishes failure to complete the legitimate task from unsafe success, and records what its tests leave unexamined.
routes.boundary: Scores from different benchmarks are not directly comparable without matching tasks, attacker access, budgets and model versions. Benchmark coverage does not prove deployment safety.
questions: Do benchmark failures predict failures in long-running real workflows?
How can adaptive attacks, utility and uncertainty be reported together?

readings.why: Makes distinct safety properties measurable in controlled environments.
readings.title: AI Safety Gridworlds

readings.why: Pairs legitimate tool tasks with security objectives in an extensible environment.
readings.title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents

readings.why: Provides a broad set of agent environments and failure modes to examine coverage.
readings.title: Agent-SafetyBench: Evaluating the Safety of LLM Agents

routes.angle: Choose what to measure before comparing defenses.

routes.intro: Red teaming actively searches for failures under an explicit attacker model. It helps discover cases that a fixed test set misses, but its conclusions depend on attack budgets, allowed access and how successes are checked.
routes.boundary: Failure discovery and prevalence estimation are different tasks. A strong attack demonstrates vulnerability under its conditions; an unsuccessful search is not a general safety guarantee.
questions: Can attack generation avoid sharing the defender’s blind spots?
How do attack success rates change with budget and adaptation?

readings.why: Uses language models to generate test cases for another model, exploring diversity and difficulty.
readings.title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models

readings.why: Offers concrete multi-step malicious tasks for studying agent misuse and jailbreak robustness.
readings.title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents

routes.angle: Search for failures under an explicit attacker model.

routes.intro: An agent can cause harm without a malicious user or injected instruction. Ambiguous requests, incorrect state estimates, planning mistakes, overconfident tool use and unintended side effects all matter in ordinary workflows.
routes.boundary: Task failure is not always a safety failure, and task success is not always safe. Define the harmful consequence and who bears it, including effects outside the immediate task metric.
questions: Can an agent recognize missing information and ask before taking a risky action?
Which recovery strategies prevent small execution errors from cascading?

readings.why: Frames accident risks from misspecified objectives, limited supervision and distribution shift.
readings.title: Concrete Problems in AI Safety

readings.why: Studies risky tool-use failures in emulated environments, including difficult-to-stage scenarios.
readings.title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox

routes.angle: Study harmful outcomes without assuming an attacker.

examples.text: Build a black-box safety monitor for tool-using agents
Stop poisoned memories from affecting later agent tasks
Protect browser agents from malicious web instructions
Evaluate collusion and unsafe delegation between agents
